searchText: yeah, I'm still a bit torn between `validator` and `deposit` as the command category. I support preparing validators as offline files by specifying a`--dont-send` flag in the `deposits create` command. You then have a separate `deposits send` command that works with offline files As a side note, when we create a validator deposit we drop a `eth1-deposit-tx-hash.txt` file alongside the keypairs so we can (a) avoid double deposits and (b) check on the transaction later. I expand on it a little here: https://notes.ethereum.org/Xh_8uIRlQnyKAxCzFMBAMw#Optional-Feature-Eth1-Deposit-Tx-Hashes Thoughts on having an accounts command instead of just validator create <@361447803194441738> ? We’re trying to emulate geth as much as possible to help users with muscle memory and they do “geth accounts new” as well as list, import, export So you can have validator accounts new, validator deposits (a separate subcommand as its own namespace), etc. oh yeah sorry, it's `lighthouse account wallet ...` and `lighthouse account validator ...` Ah perfect I think it's `account` at the moment, but can easily add `accounts` alias. Makes sense > We’re trying to emulate geth as much as possible to help users with muscle memory and they do “geth accounts new” as well as list, import, export I don't think that emulating Geth here is worth much at all. Client account management has been on the way out for years and users have been repeatedly told to not use Ethereum clients for key (account) management, so hopefully very few users are actually familiar with those commands. <@311971895828283393> It’s nothing out of this world, it’s just basic account command structure that many users of our client have been asking for <@301186049323958275> What do you propose instead? Ugh. Why are users asking for a syntax that aligns with a tool that they shouldn't be using! new, list, import, export seem pretty straightforward to me. What do you suggest instead? No cli at all? Nothing in particular, I was _only_ arguing against "Geth muscle memory" as a design goal. Having it look/feel like a tool no one should be using doesn't seem like a good design goal to me. If you happen to land on a syntax that looks similar because it is otherwise a good design then that is fine, just don't **target** Geth compatibility. We’re not doing it exactly how geth implements these things, they’re just 4 simple commands. If you have an alternative, would love to hear it I understand your rationale, we’ll keep that in mind I'm generally against CLIs ~~for this sort of thing~~, so I'm not a good person to ask for CLI design ideas. 😉 This discussion was about cli’s though How users will interact with a client to interact with accounts Yep, and my *only* feedback is that there should be 0 geth account management users if security advocacy groups have done their job well. 😄 I see, thanks Personally, I would much rather see clients serve up a little web app for account management so regular users can use it. The average mom/pop isn't likely open a CLI to do anything. They'll double click on installer and then open a shortcut added to desktop, start menu, applications folder, etc. (depending on OS). If that shortcut takes them to a docs page on how to use a CLI, they'll be lost, but if it takes the to a nice account management UI you *may* retain them. Definitely, but that doesnt mean a cli is optional Eh... I *personally* think CLIs are optional, but d recognize that I'm kind of alone among developers on that front. I much prefer GUI + API endpoint. IMO CLI is necessary for enterprise deployments What about provisioning all that stuff in cloud environments and cloud deployments? CLI is this weird middle ground for highly technical non-programmers. How would you administer everything in k8s for example if you needed to open a web app to do everything An API. Building a custom api as well seems intense When you could just use a cli like normal No different from building a CLI. For example, almost all of my docker container interactions with deployed services is done through either built-in web GUIs or API commands from scripts (almost always over HTTPS). I imagine a lot of folks would be frustrated if there were no way to administer our client except through an API You mean through a CLI? > API commands from scripts I.e., a CLI app? > I imagine a lot of folks would be frustrated if there were no way to administer our client except through an API I suspect this is true, I just think those people (who outnumber people who share my thinking by a large margin) are silly. 😄 I feel like this conversation is becoming more about personal opinions than anything else Thats a huge number of silly people I'm totally fine with dropping the conversation. The only piece I really care about is that we don't have Geth CLI compatibility as a design target because that **should** have zero users. Makes sense, thanks for the input <@311971895828283393> is right, the rest is just opinion and you shouldn't do what I say at the cost of your users on that front.

excerpts.author: zahary.
excerpts.content: yeah, I'm still a bit torn between `validator` and `deposit` as the command category. I support preparing validators as offline files by specifying a`--dont-send` flag in the `deposits create` command. You then have a separate `deposits send` command that works with offline files

excerpts.author: paulhauner
excerpts.content: As a side note, when we create a validator deposit we drop a `eth1-deposit-tx-hash.txt` file alongside the keypairs so we can (a) avoid double deposits and (b) check on the transaction later.

excerpts.author: paulhauner
excerpts.content: I expand on it a little here: https://notes.ethereum.org/Xh_8uIRlQnyKAxCzFMBAMw#Optional-Feature-Eth1-Deposit-Tx-Hashes

> We’re trying to emulate geth as much as possible to help users with muscle memory and they do “geth accounts new” as well as list, import, export
I don't think that emulating Geth here is worth much at all.  Client account management has been on the way out for years and users have been repeatedly told to not use Ethereum clients for key (account) management, so hopefully very few users are actually familiar with those commands.
